Subject: Performance SLOs & concurrency follow-up (post-demo)

Thanks again for taking the demo today — great conversation. Summary + open items below so we have a clear path for procurement.

Quick recap of customer goals (from today's call):
- Latency: p95 target ~250-300ms for short text generation (single-turn responses)
- Throughput: support peak traffic patterns for holiday promotions (spiky)
- Concurrency: ~400 concurrent end-user sessions expected at peak
- Streaming: chat UX requires streaming (progressive tokens) with low first-byte latency

What we heard from your side: average response ~50–80 tokens, 60 tokens typical; a few heavy prompts (>=1k tokens) from admin flows.

Redwood notes / capabilities:
- We can achieve the stated p95 on our Dedicated pools for curated model variants; hosted tier can also meet with request routing and autoscale but we'd want to pin capacity for predictability.
- Concurrency mapping: 400 concurrent user sessions typically maps to ~300–400 parallel in-flight model requests depending on client-side multiplexing and streaming behavior.
- Rate limits: we support per-API-key quotas and per-project rate limits (RPS and token/sec). We also support burst windows for traffic spikes.

Proposed next steps for qualification / procurement:
1) Can you confirm: expected sustained QPS during peak minute and expected average tokens per request?
2) Do you require strict hard-rate limits (requests rejected) or prefer soft throttling (queueing + 429 when full)?
3) Is streaming required for all chat surfaces or only front-line customer sessions?
4) Procurement contact so we can send the SLA/quote.

A couple of quick options we can propose once we have the answers:
- Option A (Reserved Dedicated pool): provision a dedicated pool sized for 400 concurrent requests (we’ll propose GPU count after Rishi’s calc) + guaranteed SLO + burst buffer.
- Option B (Hosted + committed quota): start with hosted; set a guaranteed quota (e.g., 200 RPS sustained with 500 RPS burst) and increase as you validate.

Attached: call-notes-20260220.txt (light notes).

Thanks — I’ll loop in Rishi for the sizing calc and Dev for the security/procurement points.

Thanks, Marissa — appreciate the clear recap. A few clarifications from our side:
- Latency: We can relax p95 to 300ms for the first phase if that helps sizing. The priority is a consistent user experience; tail latency kills conversion.
- Concurrency: 400 concurrent *end-user sessions* is the expected peak. Many sessions are idle-waiting during typing, but we need the system to support 400 active streaming sessions (we estimate ~0.8 requests/session/minute during heavy bursts).
- Tokens: ~60 tokens average, but admin/insights flows can be ~800–1,200 tokens occasionally.
- Streaming: required for customer-facing chat UI (first-byte within ~200ms ideally). Admin/analytics routes can be non-streaming.

Procurement: looped in procurement; they’ll need a formal SLA + per-minute and per-key rate limit details before we draft a PO. Can you send an initial SLA + a recommended per-key limit? Also please include a proposed billing ramp (committed vs. overage).

Adding some technical detail to map their requirements into Redwood capacity and rate-limit recommendations.

1) Concurrency -> parallel requests conversion
- If each active session produces 0.8 requests/minute at burst, 400 sessions => ~320 requests/minute => ~5.3 RPS sustained during that burst minute. However, streaming sessions keep connections open longer (first-byte latency matters). The real concurrency we size for is "in-flight" requests, not sessions; streaming increases in-flight duration.

2) Example capacity calc (back-of-envelope)
- Avg tokens/request: 60 tokens => with model X (baseline throughput), a single A100-like GPU can serve ~150–300 parallel low-latency streaming requests depending on batchability and KV cache hits.
- For predictable p95 <=300ms on streaming at that token size, recommend starting with a dedicated pool of 3–4 GPUs and autoscale policy to add +1 GPU for spikes.

3) Rate-limit recommendation (negotiable)
- Per-project quota: 200 RPS sustained, burst to 500 RPS for short windows (1–5 minutes).
- Per-API-key connection limit: 200 concurrent connections (prevents one key from monopolizing).
- Hard limits: we usually enforce hard request limits at RPS > burst window; for user experience we can do soft queueing for spikes and then return 429s when queues exceed threshold.
- Token limits: max tokens per request 4,000 (can be raised for admin flows).

4) Operational notes
- Prefix caching: if your UX reuses prompts or system messages we’ll get high KV cache hit rates, reducing GPU load significantly.
- Streaming tuning: client-side should use a single persistent connection per active session (connection pooling) and multiplex logically to avoid opening many TLS sessions.

I can run a quick load test if they can give a small traffic replay (anonymized) — the log-sample-requests.jsonl attached is the type of data that helps.

Alex / Procurement team — attaching a draft SLA and a short quote that reflects the options we discussed. High-level summary below and where we need quick confirmation so we can produce a PO-ready doc.

Summary of proposed commercial/ops items:
- Recommended start (safest): Hosted + Committed Quota
  - Committed quota: 200 RPS sustained, with a 5-minute burst allowance up to 500 RPS.
  - Per-API-key connection limit: 200 concurrent connections.
  - Token limit per request: default 4k tokens; admin flows on request.
  - Billing: monthly committed units + overage at negotiated per-token rate.
- Alternative: Dedicated Reserved Pool
  - Dedicated pool sized for 3–4 GPUs with autoscale + burst buffer. SLA-backed latency targets (p95 <=300ms for the configured model), suitable if you need deterministic performance for promotions.

Open items we need from you to finalize SLA/quote:
1) Confirm which option you prefer (Hosted + quota OR Dedicated).
2) Confirm expected average tokens per request during peak and expected sustained QPS for a peak minute.
3) Confirm whether you want soft throttling or hard rate-limit enforcement.
4) Procurement contact for contractual exchange (if procurement prefers a redline, send it to procurement@redwood.ai).

Attachments: SLA-proposal-Redwood-Acme-20260223.pdf (SLA + commercial terms), log-sample-requests.jsonl (anonymized sample format).

Related links: HubSpot deal (https://hubspot.company/deal/ACME-2026-REDWOOD-01), SLA draft (https://app.redwood.ai/agreements/ACME-SLA-draft).
